sections.overview: A Czech survey recorded this species in the Bílé Karpaty only from historical records.
sections.identification: In Britain it is the largest tabanid, with a body about 25–30 mm long and a wingspan reaching 50 mm.
sections.habitat: The species account used here places it mainly in western Britain and records it as very rare in Northern Ireland.
sections.diet: As in other tabanids, adult females take blood meals to produce eggs.
sections.behavior: The cited UK account says this very large species rarely bites people, unlike the more familiar smaller horseflies.
sections.reproduction: A study of females in eastern Croatia specifically examined the species’ gonotrophic cycle.
sections.ecology: Tabanid larvae develop in wet habitats.
sections.conservation: The account gives no species-specific status for T. sudeticus.
